CNET Survey: $75 Billion in Packages Could Be at Risk of Holiday Porch Theft

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Big holiday sales, like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, are here, but before you click ‘buy,’ make sure you have a plan to protect your package from porch pirates.
  • CNET’s annual package theft survey polls US adults about their experiences with porch pirates and how they try to prevent thefts.
  • Sources indicate that but leaving your packages up for grabs could be a massive risk — especially when thieves know holiday gifts are being delivered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Big holiday sales, like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, are here, but before you click ‘buy,’ make sure you have a plan to protect your package from porch pirates.

CNET’s annual package theft survey polls US adults about their experiences with porch pirates and how they try to prevent thefts. This year, the average package value is $276.24, and 28% of US adults have had a package stolen, know someone who has or caught an attempted theft within the past year. Yet 20% of US adults don’t use security devices due to hardware costs or monthly subscription fees.

Sources indicate that but leaving your packages up for grabs could be a massive risk — especially when thieves know holiday gifts are being delivered. On the other hand, some bad actors don’t seem to mind being caught in the act on home security cameras, so are they really enough to deter bad actors? And what more can you do to protect your deliveries?

According to recent reports, CNET’s findings show that some US adults have dealt with porch theft firsthand: 8% had packages meant for themselves or their households stolen within the past year, and 5% had a delivered gift stolen. Very few (1%) caught a theft in the act on a video doorbell or security camera.

Meanwhile, many US adults know someone who fell victim to package theft — 13% know a neighbor or community member who had a package stolen within the past year, and 12% know someone who doesn’t live in their community who has.

“Close to a third of our respondents are personally acquainted with package theft, which is still a high number compared to other concerns like break-ins,” mentioned CNET’s senior home security editor, Tyler Lacoma. “Thieves generally look for crimes of opportunity, and few things are easier than a package left on a doorstep, especially if nobody is home.”.

Surprisingly, most US adults (72%) haven’t experienced package theft or know anyone who has.

Even though the percentages above may seem low, Lacoma stated that package theft typically increases during the holidays when thieves know more deliveries are likely, and newly introduced porch theft tactics are always on the horizon.

It has been revealed that there are reports of thieves trying Wi-Fi jamming to disable live security camera footage while they steal packages. And findings show that some are installing spy cams in high-value neighborhoods to learn your home’s layout and habits to take your packages shortly after they’re delivered. In recent years, pirates have even tracked shipping labels for high-value tech, like iPhones, to steal the package within minutes of arrival.

Industry observers note that so while the majority of US adults haven’t fallen victim, that shouldn’t be a sign to shrug off the concern or relax your home security measures. Instead, now’s the time to strategy how to safely store your packages if they’re delivered while you’re away.

Online shopping and deliveries to your door can be a convenient way to check off holiday wish lists, but the average package value this holiday season is less than last year. CNET found that US adults plan to have an average of $276.24 in holiday packages delivered during this holiday season. That’s $23.82 less than last year’s average of $300.06.

By generation, Millennials also have a lower estimated average package value than last year, with an average of $227.25, compared to their 2025 package value of $307.47 — an $80.22 difference, while Gen Z’s package value is only about $7 less than last year. But any package’s value is still worth taking precautions to help prevent it from being stolen.

Sources indicate that lacoma has thoughts on why that might be. In short, lower spending could mean fewer packages.

Sources indicate that “I wonder if people have also simply gotten fewer packages in general this year due to tariffs, inflation and tech prices. That could pull these numbers down,” said Lacoma. But there’s a high chance that could be the case considering CNET’s 2026 annual holiday survey, which found that US adult tech spending is down to $808 — which is $123 less than last year’s average of $931.

Thieves may not always know what’s in boxes they’re stealing but they’re willing to take a chance. We asked US adults which items were stolen in package thefts in the past year to give you a sense of what’s at risk.

Recent findings suggest that among the items stolen, apparel and accessories were the most common goods stolen (40%). That’s followed by toys and games (23%). Then there are everyday home basics, like decor, cookware and small appliances (19%).

But personal tech devices and accessories are still among the items stolen. Small accessories like phone chargers and cases are most common (16%) among tech-related packages stolen. They are followed by audio gadgets like headphones and Bluetooth speakers, along with streaming devices and soundbars (11%, respectively).

Still, more costly tech like gaming consoles (10%), computers and laptops (9%) and smart home devices (6%) are among devices stolen.

You shouldn’t leave your packages up to chance. That’s why Lacoma recommends a few safer options to ensure your packages are stored securely after they’re delivered, even beyond keeping an eye on your doorbell or security camera. Instead, keep your packages out of sight with tactics like a delivery box with a code or key or ask for an in-garage delivery.

It has been revealed that “Delivery boxes have reached a upcoming level of popularity in recent years as an effective way to stop porch pirates completely. However, Amazon’s Key service that delivers to your garage is an alternative,” stated Lacoma. “Either way, you’ll need to trust delivery people to handle your shipments, unless you want to arrange for pickup at a nearby shipping center, which some people like to combine with other holiday errands.”.

If you don’t want to install a latest security feature, try scheduling your packages to arrive when you know you’re home, requiring a signature from someone you trust or changing your delivery location to a pickup spot, like UPS’ Hold for Pick-Up locations or Amazon Lockers.

Home surveillance, like outdoor security cameras and video doorbells, can deter package thieves who don’t want to risk getting caught on camera. But US adults have mixed feelings about their effectiveness in protecting against package theft.

There are two deterrents that are keeping US adults from having security devices — cost and privacy. Findings show that 20% of US adults lack home security measures due to hardware costs or monthly subscription fees. That’s followed by 9% who don’t want to use cameras because of privacy concerns.

It has been revealed that “Fortunately, the right home security picks can solve both these problems,” said Lacoma. “Brands like Tapo, Eufy, Aqara and even Google Nest offer package detection and alerts for free, so you don’t have to worry about extra fees.”.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a camera that’s off-the-grid, consider the Arlo Go 2. It’s an LTE camera, so it uses a cellular data connection instead of Wi-Fi. It still finds a signal, supports app operation and live video viewing. If you’re looking for a power-over-Ethernet camera that uses a cable connection, the Reolink Duo 3 is a good choice.

It has been revealed that lacoma added that many companies also offer ways to use local video storage and local AI detection so nothing is stored in the cloud. There are also features, such as customizable privacy zones, to minimize privacy concerns when used with the right precautions.

In a recent development, among all US adults, only 14% have security devices with a monthly subscription that lets them save or playback video. By comparison, 12% have security devices but no subscription.

Those percentages could be low for a few reasons, including the overall perception of how helpful surveillance and security really are against porch theft. Eleven percent of US adults don’t think security devices deter porch thefts. It’s a valid concern since 4% fell victim to package theft or an attempted theft despite having security devices. And some US adults (9%) use security devices to get proof of a theft after the fact — not to prevent it.

In a recent development, but that doesn’t mean you should ignore the possibility of package theft — especially during the holidays. Even if you don’t want to install cameras or latest security devices, make a plan to protect your packages and avoid the headache of package theft over the holidays.

“Remember, the simple presence of a security camera is enough to make many thieves look elsewhere – interviews have confirmed it,” said Lacoma. “And with today’s phone alerts about package detection, you can usually check on a package only seconds after it appears, or bring up footage if it unexpectedly vanishes, letting you take action fast. New practices like delivery boxes or in-garage delivery help address risks in concrete ways, too.”.

It has been revealed that CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,016 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Oct. 23–27, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus).

The $75 billion figure was calculated by multiplying the average value of deliveries each US adult expects to receive by the 2025 US population of adults ages 18 and over calculated by the US Census Bureau.

Sources indicate that retailers that use AI shopping agents are seeing bigger orders and more loyal customers. The survey found that shoppers who use AI agent referrals are twice as likely to make a purchase. In addition, 39% of shoppers have used AI agents on an e-commerce site, and 80% had a positive experience, while 75% felt more loyal to the brand as a result of the AI agent experience.

In a recent development, 1 in 3 consumers has used an AI agent, including the widely adopted Meta Muse, now used by 12% of all consumers. Grok Bot is also in high demand.

The survey found that 28% of consumers give their agents multiple tasks per day. The most common use of AI agents is price comparisons, product reviews, and brainstorming for gift items. Brand discovery is a major benefit of AI agent use cases.

Agents as advisors are growing, but agents are not buying products yet, with only 19% of personal agent people using logic to check out. Only 9% of consumers allow their personal AI agents to have unrestricted access to their financial details, and 36% have set up a separate credit card for their AI agents.

Also: ZDNET’s favorite tech devices for 2026.

It has been revealed that the majority of consumers (73%) are not comfortable giving personal AI agents their payment information, and 49% are not interested in agents making purchases on their behalf. Consumers do not want to share their purchase history or personal data that could potentially lead to unwanted charges. Shoppers will abandon an AI agent after 2-3 mistakes. If an AI agent makes a bad recommendation, 1 in 3 consumers will blame the AI.

Sources indicate that retailers must adopt AI shopping agents in order to compete. Retailers must be able to service and respond to shopper agents. The ability to detect intent, buying signals, sources of dissatisfaction, and other consumer-related buying patterns at machine scale (significantly faster and higher volume than human scale) will require retailers to invest in AI agentic engagement capabilities.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well.

Today, AI agents advise consumers on their holiday shopping journeys, but in the very near future, they will autonomously make purchasing decisions with little to no involvement from their human counterparts.   • The tool changer technology also allows you to mix different materials with less of a fuss, so you can use a typical rigid plastic and something like a flexible rubber in a single pass without stopping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday, Bambu Lab took the wraps off its third-generation 3D printer, the P3C. It brings to the mainstream the company’s “tool changer” technology, which was previously reserved for higher-end, flagship models like the $2,500 H3C. Given the P3C costs less than half the bigger model, it might be the perfect gift to get your favorite 3D printing hobbyist for Black Friday.

The big deal here is the introduction of the Swaptek 7-tool changer, which allows you to switch to a different color or material in just 6 seconds, preventing you from having to stop and clean the nozzle every time. The technology produces significantly less waste and allows you to create faster prints.

The tool changer technology also allows you to mix different materials with less of a fuss, so you can use a typical rigid plastic and something like a flexible rubber in a single pass without stopping. It can switch between different nozzle sizes in one job. You can switch between  0.2 mm, 0.4 mm, 0.6 mm and 0.8 mm midprint.

Industry observers note that the P3C ships with an integrated sealed AMS 3P filament management system that can store up to seven spools, each of which is on an independent feed path to the printer. You can also connect up to four external AMS units, supporting up to 22 colors.

According to recent reports, the P3C is more than just a 3D printer. The Swaptek system supports interchangeable craft tools, letting you cut, draw or emboss on materials.

Industry observers note that bambu Lab also included a few features that make the P3C more approachable to newcomers. The P3C provides full-auto calibration, automatically aligning nozzle offsets and multi-tool heads so you don’t have to do it yourself. There’s also a built-in AI monitoring system that can detect issues like nozzle clogs and purge-bin jams early on. A fresh health management system will no longer spit out vague or obscure errors when something goes wrong. Instead, the new system will explain the problem in plain language and provide step-by-step troubleshooting right on the screen.

CNET’s 3D printing expert, James Bricknell, hasn’t been able to test Bambu Labs’ latest model yet but is excited about it. “While the P3C didn’t arrive in time for a hands-on, it’s built with the same design language and hardware support as the recently released H3C. If it is anywhere near as good, and I think that’s likely, it’ll be at the top of any serious 3D printing enthusiast’s wish list.”.

The P3C 3D printer AMS combo is available now worldwide for $1,149. The combo includes the printer, AMS 3P as well as 5 0.4mm standard PrintTools. Two slots are left open for you to customize. This combo option comes with virtually everything you need to get started printing your works of art and more.

If Tasks sounds familiar, it should: The tech giant already has a product called Google Tasks, which lets you turn emails into a checkable to-do list on the side of your inbox, among other places like Chat and Docs. This is the agentic version, obviously.

In a recent development, gewirtz, ZDNET’s AI tester-in-residence, wasn’t blown away by then-Spark when he tried it last month, but had reason to believe in its eventual improvement. It’s unclear whether Tasks is meaningfully different from Spark, aside from being out of beta.

Recent findings suggest that abilities aside, what sets Tasks apart here is cost. Dots and Duet haven’t exactly impressed thus far, so free alternatives don’t have a high bar to reach yet.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks.

During Gewirtz’s test, when the agent was part of his $20 per month Google AI Pro plan, he used only 20% of the total five hours of usage on “four fairly substantial tests.” Without an AI plan, Gemini’s context window is 32k tokens.

According to recent reports, at launch in September, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Muse is “free to use for up to 100M tokens per week,” though Meta’s help center is not so explicit. As with most agentic products, more frequent people may want to buy more access, but more casual users now have two options to compare.

AI companies are vying to hook customers with their various personal agents, and price and privacy are major factors to consider. Being free with limits, Muse and Tasks are perhaps geared toward a more apprehensive user who wants to try an agent, but isn’t giving it countless tasks to take on all day. #166810. A Human and an AI Model (Apparently) Solved the Riemann Hypothesis: What it Means for Future of Math

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2186 w)

A Human and an AI Model (Apparently) Solved the Riemann Hypothesis: What it Means for Future of Math

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Riemann Hypothesis is one of math’s oldest and most famous unsolved problems.
  • Alpöge made the announcement on Friday in a four-page document (PDF) on his personal web page.
  • Sources indicate that “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge said in the announcement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Riemann Hypothesis is one of math’s oldest and most famous unsolved problems. It was originally put forward as a problem in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, and professional and amateur mathematicians alike have made thousands of attempts to solve it. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge has apparently solved the problem with the help of AI, showing that in the battle of humans versus AI, the real winner might be both of them working together.

Alpöge made the announcement on Friday in a four-page document (PDF) on his personal web page.

Sources indicate that “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge said in the announcement. “In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too.”.

The actual hypothesis itself isn’t the biggest deal since all it does is make it easier to see the distribution of prime numbers. However, math didn’t come to a screeching halt just because the hypothesis hadn’t been proven. There are hundreds of other math theorems along with algorithms and cryptographic encryption methods that operate based on the assumption that the Riemann Hypothesis is true.

The Riemann Hypothesis is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Problems for this very reason. If Alpöge really did solve the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude’s help, it would remove a metaphorical logjam that’s been gumming up the works for over a century and a half. Most of those hundreds of math theorems would be proven as true overnight, and all of those algorithms and encryption methods would be validated. That would make solving the Riemann Hypothesis one of the greatest mathematical breakthroughs in history.

It has been revealed that “It is certainly an exciting time,” Paul Milewski, head of the department of mathematics at Penn State, said in an email to CNET. “The Riemann Hypothesis (or any big theorem) is often not the ‘goal’ of mathematics. They are set up as grand challenges that require the development of new tools, new results along the way and new understanding. It is the ‘voyage’ and not the destination that matters the most.”.

As such, the mathematics community wasted no time testing the proof to see whether it was true. Two groups — Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative — independently verified the proof, with many other researchers running their own tests and coming to the same conclusion.

“We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on the achievement,” the two groups noted in a joint statement on Saturday.

This is certainly an exciting discovery, but it’s not without its obstacles. Alpöge’s proof was a staggering 250,000 pages of some of the most complex math ever written by a human or a machine. Alpöge provided 17 million lines of Lean code, a programming language specifically made for writing and checking proofs, and that’s how researchers were able to check the work and show it to be true.

It has been revealed that the problem is that the average novel is about 300 pages, and that means that Alpöge’s AI-assisted proof is approximately 833 novels’ worth of complex math. For reference, the longest work ever produced is World-2023, which holds the Guinness World Record at 100,100 pages. That book is 19 feet tall, and Alpöge’s proof is two and a half times longer.

In a recent development, despite the logic being verified as true through Lean code, Alpöge still has a major problem. So far, none of the mathematicians or researchers who have attempted to read it have been able to understand what it says.

“I do not understand, and I suspect no human completely understands,” Jon Keating, professor of mathematical physics at the University of Oxford, mentioned in a Numberphile YouTube video. “When I look at that, I’m completely in awe and in wonderment.”.

According to recent reports, for the problem to be fully solved, the proof has to be read, analyzed and simplified so that it can be translated into readable mathematics, which Alpöge says in his announcement that he’s in the process of doing. All of this has to be done so that Alpöge can publish it in a peer-reviewed journal in such a way that his peers can actually read it. It is only after the mathematics community scrutinizes and accepts Alpöge’s proof that it is considered fully solved.

Aside from being nigh unreadable to humans, Alpöge has otherwise avoided the kinds of drama that other AI-assisted discoveries have faced in 2026.

Sources indicate that openAI had to backtrack on its proof of the Navier-Stokes problem, which is another Millennium Problem, after the organization couldn’t rule out that the AI models it used had access to data from other researchers. Somewhat ironically, one of those mathematicians whose work OpenAI may have  — knowingly or unknowingly — borrowed from was Levent Alpöge, as he and others were pretty close to solving the problem on their own.

Similarly, Claude was credited with finding a new novel enzyme that humans had never seen before. The problem is that computational biologist Mario Rodríguez Mestre had seen this enzyme before and was using Claude to study it further, so it’s uncertain if Claude actually found it independently or used data from Mestre’s research to find it.

In a recent development, the heavy assistance from AI has been met with mostly positive reactions, with most researchers agreeing that the AI usage is justified provided that the proof is proven to be true through peer review. Since no one was particularly close to solving the Riemann Hypothesis, there haven’t been any accusations of Alpöge or Claude stealing work like those prior examples. By and large, most mathematicians are excited about the discovery.

Recent findings suggest that “Even before this, we have seen the power of AI, and this highlights that AI trained on hundreds of years of human mathematics can perform amazing tasks,” said Penn State’s Milewski. “I would add that AI didn’t come up with the Riemann Hypothesis, nor did most of the work to prove it, and AI probably doesn’t ‘know’ why it was invented or why it’s important.”.

Sources indicate that CNET spoke with a few professors about this, and they all echoed Milewski’s sentiment, stating that AI was trained with centuries of human mathematical achievement, so a win for AI is a win for humans too. Jeffrey Lagarias, a professor of mathematics at the University of Michigan, told CNET that “I don’t think this particular proof would have been found without AI.”.

Sources indicate that prasad Tetali, head of the department of mathematical sciences at Carnegie Mellon University, mentioned: “It is easy to overestimate the role of AI, and underappreciate decades of human mathematician work that went into it. The AI here is really standing tall and wide on the shoulders of generations of human giants.”.

On the AI side of things, influencers are attempting to use the news to hype up the capabilities of AI. Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang mentioned in a post on X that solving the Riemann Hypothesis was a sign that AI superintelligence was close at hand and that humanity should be terrified of the “alien mind that we don’t understand.”.

AI researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky likened the whole thing to a organization making enriched uranium that’ll one day result in the end of the human species.

These warnings are hard to take seriously when one considers that Anthropic tried to make Claude solve the Riemann Hypothesis by itself back in August. Claude came up with some cool ideas but ultimately failed to solve the problem alone. For the time being, AI still needs a great deal of human guidance to make these massive discoveries, so the doom-and-gloom proselytizing comes off as a little premature.

It has been revealed that to make things even more interesting, a competing Riemann Hypothesis proof was submitted by Alessandro Masullo just a few hours after Alpöge released his. This competing proof is 940 pages long, which is significantly shorter than Alpöge’s proof, and it was an all-human effort with no AI assistance. The proof is months in the making, with Masullo working with mathematician Brian Conrad to bring it up to spec before it hits peer review. When Alpöge posted his proof, Masullo and others thought it wise to submit theirs as well.

According to recent reports, this started a “dueling proofs” storyline over the weekend, but it was short-lived. Shortly after Masullo’s proof was posted, multiple people found the types of flaws and omissions that often disprove Riemann Hypothesis proofs. Those issues are in the process of being corrected, and the proof is officially in mid-revision status.

Masullo kept the original proof posted (PDF) in its unedited form, but acknowledges that the proof was rushed to publication so that it could compete with Alpöge and Claude.

“The PDF below was posted on Nov. 20 on Ravi Vakil’s blog,” Masullo wrote on a Google site. “It was never meant to be shared publicly at this stage, and it has been posted in this draft form in response to current circumstances.”.

It’s entirely possible that future revisions of Masullo’s work may solve the problems in the early draft and create a fully human proof of the Riemann Hypothesis without AI, but that isn’t happening anytime soon.

It has been revealed that this is a lot of information about finding the Riemann Hypothesis, so it’s probably a good idea to briefly explain what it even is. In the 1730s, famous mathematician Leonhard Euler came up with a zeta function as a way to solve the Basel Problem, another mathematical curiosity about the exact sum of the reciprocals of squares. Euler was successful in this endeavor, and the zeta function became a part of mathematics.

Sources indicate that bernhard Riemann picked up where Euler left off and expanded the zeta function to use complex numbers — real numbers mixed with imaginary numbers — using a process called analytic continuation. Riemann used this expanded function to express how many prime numbers there were under a specific number and how tightly those prime numbers were packed together.

This is easy enough to do in your head with small numbers, like figuring out there are four prime numbers under 10, but when the biggest prime number is 41,024,320 digits long, having a function to do it for you is a lot more helpful.

The mechanics of Riemann’s expanded zeta function are quite complicated, and the math-focused YouTube channel Numberphile has an excellent explainer from a professional mathematician (with pictures) if you want to learn more.

The hypothesis concerns the solutions the function yields. Riemann’s version of the zeta function showed that if you plugged in an even negative number, like -2, -4 or -672, the function would always spit out a zero. These are referred to as trivial zeroes, and Riemann proved that this was always true in his original paper.

The Riemann Hypothesis is the conjecture that all the other numbers that would also make a zero — referred to as non-trivial zeroes — follow a very specific formula, which is “½ + it”, where “i” is an imaginary number and “t” is any real number, positive or negative. In short, Riemann believed that there was no other way to generate a zero with his zeta function other than even negative numbers (trivial zeroes) and numbers that followed the “½+it” formula (non-trivial zeroes). Riemann provided some examples of the hypothesis being right but never wrote a full proof of it.

Recent findings suggest that it’s worth noting that not every number that follows the “½+it” formula produces a zero, but that all the numbers that produce a zero will use that formula. It’s kind of the same as saying that all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares.

In a recent development, in the 167 years since the hypothesis was first published, mathematicians have found 12 trillion non-trivial zeroes, and every single one of them fits the above rules. Trillions of other numbers that don’t follow those rules have been tested to find a counterexample, since even one counterexample disproves the hypothesis immediately. Those efforts have produced no counterexamples at all.

In a recent development, this isn’t conclusive proof, but it’s such an overwhelming amount of evidence that mathematicians began assuming that the hypothesis was true, even if no one could prove it. Alpöge’s AI-assisted proof is the first to show in any context that the hypothesis is always true, which, according to Tetali, has implications in prime number understanding, number theory and other branches of mathematics.

Industry observers note that “The major job on the math side is to find a human-understandable proof,” Lagarias said. “I would say this is certainly going to happen; there will be such understanding. Already there are several AI digests of the proof breaking it into its component pieces. I have seen one [that’s] 11 pages, 164 pages, 273 pages. There are great ideas to extract from them.”.

Industry News: An Unsecured Database Exposed About 2 Billion Login Records

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A database containing about 2 billion login records for sites across the internet was accessible online without a password, security researcher Jeremiah Fowler mentioned in a report published Tuesday by ExpressVPN.
  • The 2 billion figure is an estimate and not representative of the number of people affected, since some accounts may appear more than once and one person can have dozens of logins saved on a single device.
  • It has been revealed that fowler’s estimate of about 2 billion login records applies to the database he found.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A database containing about 2 billion login records for sites across the internet was accessible online without a password, security researcher Jeremiah Fowler mentioned in a report published Tuesday by ExpressVPN. The collection included usernames and passwords tied to email, social media, shopping and financial services. Among the files was an ad offering access to email accounts sorted by geography.

The 2 billion figure is an estimate and not representative of the number of people affected, since some accounts may appear more than once and one person can have dozens of logins saved on a single device. Fowler reported the database to its hosting provider, which restricted public access several days later. It’s unclear how long the files had been exposed or who else may have accessed them.

It has been revealed that fowler’s estimate of about 2 billion login records applies to the database he found. Wired put the total at more than 3.5 billion by including a separate database that security firm UpGuard disclosed last week. That database held about 1.64 billion records, including Chinese national ID numbers, phone numbers and school enrollment records.

Some of the files Fowler reviewed appeared to be from infostealers — malicious software that collects saved passwords and other data from infected devices. Once that information is collected, brokers can buy it in bulk, sort it by country or account type and resell it in smaller batches. A buyer interested in email accounts in a particular country can pay for that slice of the data. The people selling it can make money from the same records more than once.

Fowler saw signs that the files came from multiple sources, but couldn’t determine who assembled the collection or whether it was used for sales, research or another purpose.

I saw a version of that business in my reporting on the dark web for CNET. On Genesis Market, buyers could shop for stolen accounts by location and category, including banking, email and social media. By the time authorities disrupted the marketplace in 2023, it had offered access to data from more than 1.5 million compromised computers, according to the Justice Department.

Recent findings suggest that you can look up your email address in Have I Been Pwned to see whether it appears in a known data exposure. A clean result only tells you what’s in the service’s index.

According to recent reports, if you see an unfamiliar login or suspect your device is infected, use a different, trusted device to change the affected password and sign out of other sessions. Start with your email if several accounts may be affected, since that’s where password reset links often go. Replace reused passwords with unique ones, use a password manager to keep track of them and turn on two-factor authentication where it’s available.

Identity theft protection services monitor for signs that your personal information has been exposed or misused. In a leak like this one, an alert about an exposed password can tell you which account to secure, especially if you’ve reused that password elsewhere. Aura is one of the services we tested for CNET’s guide to the best identity theft protection services.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Google Wallet app is available for iPhone owners in the US for the first time.
  • Also: You can use Google’s Spark AI agent, renamed Tasks, for free now – with limits.
  • Industry observers note that the newly introduced Google Wallet app lets you digitize physical cards, including payment, loyalty, and membership cards, as well as boarding passes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Google Wallet app is available for iPhone owners in the US for the first time. iOS users who download the new Google Wallet app can manage online payments for faster checkout at places that support Google Pay. However, Apple restricts Google’s ability to offer tap-to-pay service on the iOS app, so users won’t be able to use Google Wallet for contactless checkout on iPhone.

Also: You can use Google’s Spark AI agent, renamed Tasks, for free now – with limits.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced Google Wallet app lets you digitize physical cards, including payment, loyalty, and membership cards, as well as boarding passes. Google Wallet app users on iOS will also be able to view receipts and track orders pulled from Gmail in one app.

Recent findings suggest that there used to be a Google Pay app for iOS, but it was discontinued in 2024. The old Google Pay app also didn’t support tap-to-pay on iPhone, but it offered limited functionality, including support for loyalty and gift cards, as well as purchase tracking.

The biggest difference between the old Google Pay app for iOS and the new Google Wallet is the AI component, which supports agentic shopping, likely as Google’s longer-term play.

One of Google’s goals for the Wallet app on iOS is to make it a central place to manage purchases made by its AI agents. The Agents section in Google Wallet for iPhone lets you manage and monitor purchases made through Gemini.

Sources indicate that agentic commerce is on the rise, as evidenced by the growing use of Meta’s Muse. Gemini can make purchases and payments through the Tasks feature, which lets you give Gemini permission to buy the items you want and set your maximum budget.

Also: Google Wallet just turned your Android phone into a digital house key.

The Google Wallet app for iOS becomes the central hub for purchase management in agentic commerce through Gemini. In it, you can view active tasks to see which purchases Gemini is working on, as well as completed purchases and receipts.

Google has been working on two technologies to support its agentic commerce strategy: Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and Agent Payments Protocol (AP2).

UCP is a technical language that enables AI agents to communicate with retailers and make purchases, while AP2 is the payment framework that establishes rules and authorization for agents to make payments.

Google Wallet serves as both the AI-powered wallet and the consumer-facing record of transactions made by Gemini.

Also: Google Wallet has a lot of latest tricks – these 5 are my favorites.

Along with Google, major retailers supported the development of UCP, including Shopify, Walmart, Target, and Etsy. When Google declared AP2, more than 60 organizations became involved, including PayPal, Salesforce, Mastercard, and American Express.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia has had its share of drama lately, with the ousting and sudden un-ousting of CEO Jensen Huang after it was discovered he’d had multiple affairs, including one that involved an alleged member of a Chinese spy network.
  • Given that, the world’s largest semiconductor company possibly wishes its biggest problem were software-related.
  • According to recent reports, the glitch began popping up in mid-November as posts on Nvidia’s support forums, as well as on Reddit and sites like HardForum, reported seeing as much as 30GB to 70GB of data per hour written to their SSDs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia has had its share of drama lately, with the ousting and sudden un-ousting of CEO Jensen Huang after it was discovered he’d had multiple affairs, including one that involved an alleged member of a Chinese spy network. The fallout from the revelations was so significant that some worried Huang’s fate could be a major disruptor to the health of international markets and the future of the entire AI industry.

Given that, the world’s largest semiconductor company possibly wishes its biggest problem were software-related. But that won’t be much comfort to PC owners affected by a software bug in Nvidia’s graphics driver that has caused some to experience excessive writes to their solid-state drives.

According to recent reports, the glitch began popping up in mid-November as posts on Nvidia’s support forums, as well as on Reddit and sites like HardForum, reported seeing as much as 30GB to 70GB of data per hour written to their SSDs. These types of drives wear down quickly over months of such use.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment and hasn’t made any public statements on the matter, but did acknowledge it in a hotfix and subsequent software upgrade for its Windows 11 GeForce Game Ready Driver 621.40, where it mentioned under Fixed General Bugs, “Excessive writes to file nvlog.nvlgstg may occur in background.” The driver that appeared to have caused the problems was released on Nov. 12.Some tech experts on social media had been suggesting rolling back to older graphics drivers before the hotfixes were released and warned that letting the problem go unchecked could cause an SSD to eventually fail.

Described by WCCF Tech as “a hotfix for the hotfix,” the latest update appears to fix the concern in ways that the previous fix did not.

Nvidia’s software problem closely mirrors an issue AMD had with its own Adrenalin Edition graphics software just weeks ago. As of Nov. 18, AMD was still making tweaks to its graphics software to iron out any lingering problems.

PCGamer offered a way to check if your PC is affected by the excess writing issue.

According to recent reports, open Task Manager, click on the Details tab and right-click on the columns at the top to select “I/O write bytes” as one of your Task Manager columns. By doing that, you can see if the file “NVDisplay.Container.exe” is writing a huge amount of data to your data drive.

If that’s the case, you should update immediately to Nvidia’s latest drivers for the fix. In fact, it might be a good idea to update whether you’re experiencing high write rates or not, just to be safe.

90% of employers reject resumes that look like AI – yet half use AI to interview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider.
  • New data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.
  • According to recent reports, also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider. At the same time, they’re turning to AI to help screen more candidates — meaning those videos you’ve seen on the internet of people pranking AI interviewers aren’t going away anytime soon.

New data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.

According to recent reports, also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost.

“The survey data is self-reported, so it reflects what employers believe has happened, not a measured outcome,” Greenhouse’s Head of Voice AI Ophir Samson told ZDNET via email.

Employers are also reacting to AI by adjusting their hiring processes: 86% of those surveyed reported changes to account for AI’s impact. 57% of them did so by adding another human interview.

According to recent reports, “As jobseekers rely more on AI to polish and send out their job applications, employers are finding it harder to tell who’s actually right for the role,” the report stated, echoing an ongoing push-and-pull between applicants and hiring teams. AI resume screeners automatically toss a majority of applications they deem unfit, so applicants try not to get tossed by formatting their material for the screener, which then backfires anyway.

The report shows how a tough economy and an influx of AI hiring tools are colliding, arguably to benefit employers over applicants. Greenhouse noted that, ironically, AI tools are helping hiring managers while also making resumes untrustworthy, and applicants would rather be interviewed by AI than not at all.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams.

“A growing number of employers are using AI not just to filter candidates out, but to have conversations with more candidates, earlier, through AI-powered voice technology,” Greenhouse said, adding that “half now use AI interviews to hear from more candidates, and 40% of those have found strong candidates they would have missed.”.

Greenhouse itself offers a voice AI screening interview tool. Samson told ZDNET that an HR professional ran 200 candidates she’d rejected through Greenhouse’s tool, and it suggested 19.

“All five of the finalists came from that group, and she ultimately hired one from the group,” Samson said.

Industry observers note that what we don’t, and maybe can’t, know is the inverse: whether AI screeners influence hiring managers to turn away candidates they actually should have considered. At least in Greenhouse’s case, Samson remarked Voice AI doesn’t make hiring decisions or “automatically advance, reject, or rank candidates.”.

“Recruiters review every output, and one recruiter owns the outcome and can explain how they reached it,” he remarked.

Greenhouse’s report surveyed 1,347 hiring managers and recruiters across the US, UK, Germany, Australia, and Ireland from late September to mid-October, and found that half of employers using voice AI “say the early-stage candidate experience has improved.”.

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ latest top stressor.

Industry observers note that it’s unclear what “improved” means there, though, and whether applicants themselves would agree with that. Still, when given the choice, only 7% of applicants in the US would turn down an AI interview, per an earlier Greenhouse report. Additionally, “70% of those who’ve had a live AI interview say it helped them show their skills,” that report said.

Sources indicate that but how swayed is that by the state of the US job market? October’s job report was better than expected, but it’s still been a tough year overall for job-seekers. Greenhouse’s findings could be as much a reflection of how desperate applicants are as an endorsement of or comfort with AI screenings.

Sources indicate that “The job market could be a factor. Our Future of Hiring Candidate Report reveals 81% of job seekers were rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company, human or AI,” Samson said. “But I’d be careful about reading the data as desperation. Candidates are setting clear conditions: nearly half (49%) want to know if a human will review their responses and 40% want to know how they’ll be evaluated.”.

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires – and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead.

According to recent reports, samson remarked that a software engineer named Ryan Quinlan, who was hired at Blissway, initially thought “talking to an AI” sounded stranger, but that it ultimately “felt like a conversation” that let him mention skills he’d forgotten to include on his resume. Samson said that Ryan has been “a ‘maybe’ on paper,” but that the AI interview helped him get over the line to be considered.

It has been revealed that “For most applicants, a human conversation was never on the table,” Samson stated. “The real choice is a resume lost in a pile, or 15 minutes to tell their story.”.

Greenhouse found that while employers are using AI to screen more candidates, most are maintaining human oversight over the most important decisions in the hiring process.

“Of all the tasks employers would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates to advance came last, at just 7%,” Greenhouse remarked.

It has been revealed that A recent California law aims to protect employees from being fired by AI systems that make determinations about their performance without a human co-signing the assessment. As with many AI productivity tools in the workplace, proper adoption ideally equates to more time for human workers to handle more crucial tasks.

Also: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside.

“Of employers who’ve saved time with AI, 85% put it back into candidates, most often by spending more time with shortlisted candidates (45%) and interviewing more candidates earlier (40%),” Greenhouse noted.

The main question around AI interviewers remains whether they’re correctly capturing your interview the way you’d hope a human interviewer would (though that’s still deeply subjective and out of applicants’ control anyway).

In a recent development, “When AI interviews are implemented thoughtfully and transparently, they pay off for both candidates and recruiters,” Samson said. “Every candidate who uses our Voice AI can opt out, and about 90% rate the experience as excellent.”.

#166800. This Is What My Apple Watch Heard When I Let It Evesdrop on My Conversations

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1221 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

This Is What My Apple Watch Heard When I Let It Evesdrop on My Conversations

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • No, your phone isn’t listening to you.
  • Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a newly introduced set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.
  • Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No, your phone isn’t listening to you. But what about your Apple Watch? I’ve been testing newly introduced Audio Intelligence features that record conversations around me, and despite how disturbing it may sound to have your smartwatch listening and taking notes of your entire day, the reality has been a lot more mundane.

Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a newly introduced set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.

Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.

It’s similar functionality as AI-powered recording pins like Plaud or Amazon’s Bee, but within the context of your smartwatch and without the additional cost or subscription.

In a recent development, and it’s completely optional. You have to first opt-in to the features to activate them, then choose to turn the feature you want on whenever you want to start using it. Then you can leave it on all day, set it on a schedule or toggle it manually whenever you need it. If you’re like me and forget that it’s on, you get reminders that it’s still listening or to check your recaps.

The fact that you have so much control over whether you use it and how much helped ease the creepy factor for me, but there’s still everyone else to consider.

Beyond a barely audible chime when I double-click the Digital Crown to activate Live Rewind, there’s no way to alert others that the feature is in use and that whoever’s in earshot is inadvertently getting roped into my little experiment as well. Other wearables like smart glasses have an indicator light on the front to alert spectators when they’re recording video.

It has been revealed that apple has built-in privacy safeguards for the audio, how it’s processed and then deleted. I’ve broken all that down in a separate Audio Intelligence FAQ. This is about what it’s like to use it in the wild.

I’ve been testing Audio Intelligence in the WatchOS 27.3 (and iOS) public beta for two weeks. Because this isn’t the final version (Apple indicates it will release publicly later this year), consider this a sneak preview.

Let’s get Live Rewind out of the way because there’s not a lot to say about it. Whether from a lack of muscle memory (or usefulness), I’ve had to go out of my way to remember the feature exists.

Industry observers note that I figured it’d come in handy for those “come again?” moments during conversations, but the reality is that it’s just easier to ask someone to repeat what they remarked than remember to double-press the Digital Crown at just the right moment. I can see it being more useful when you’re listening to a presentation or other event.

It has been revealed that fifteen seconds go by a lot faster than I expect and by the time I realize something might be worth revisiting, the person has moved on with the conversation. I either missed what I intended to get or just captured the silence after.

Siri Recap has been more useful, though it’s still hit-or-miss. The feature gives you high-level summaries of what it heard — it doesn’t provide a transcript to review, and it doesn’t identify who said what. It shines brightest during dedicated meetings when there’s a single conversation to follow rather than a jumble of unrelated discussions.

One success story: I was moderating the chat for our iPhone Duo live folding test on YouTube while Matthew Murray, CNET’s lab director, answered viewer questions on the stream.

I thought I’d caught the gist of what he was saying, but the typing must’ve distracted me more than I realized because I was pleasantly surprised to learn some interesting facts that I’d missed in the Siri Recap, like “Opening a phone 20 times daily over 10 years equals 73,000 folds” or that the “machine runs approximately 22,560 cycles every 24 hours”.

But Siri’s batting average wasn’t always that good, which made it challenging to trust the notes. During a conversation with another mom about car-pool logistics, Siri Recap pulled out action items, like who I was picking up and at what time, which I appreciated, but the information wasn’t accurate. Not only had Siri gotten the names of the kids wrong, it also had me picking up the wrong kid. Clearly, the mental load of figuring out after-school logistics is challenging even for Siri.

Siri can’t handle the messy conversations (and TV highlights).

Where things get interesting (and occasionally hilarious) is how Siri discerns what constitutes a conversation and how many topics belong in a single recap.

Siri is generally good at accurately labeling what conversations are about: “Parent-teacher conferences,” “Car-pool logistics,” “Folding phone durability testing.” But rather than keeping them separate, as it should, it sometimes conflates two or even three completely unrelated conversations into a single recap.

It has been revealed that I encountered bullet points summarizing a serious conversation with a friend about a medical condition alongside notes about a chaotic (albeit funny) exploding apple cider incident with my kids. The two conversations happened within the same two-hour window, but they were by no means back-to-back.

It’s a good thing Siri Recap leaves out tone and volume cause that last bullet would’ve been in ALL CAPS.

What it did decide was worthy of a standalone recap was a discussion about wedding plans during an episode of Nobody Wants This on Netflix. To be fair, this would’ve absolutely warranted a recap if I’d been discussing my own wedding plans; however, the fact that the “conversation” happened at midnight should’ve tipped off Siri that this was a late-night binge session and not an actual conversation needing to be recapped.

Rather than coming away better informed about the notable conversations I’d had throughout the day, I came away feeling validated by the sheer chaos of it all. The constant whiplash of being pulled in a dozen different directions — bouncing between work, kids, gossip and the occasional sticky beverage crisis — was real and now immortalized (until the recap automatically expires if you don’t choose to save it).

Industry observers note that for now, while novel, neither Siri Recap nor Live Rewind is reason enough to buy (or avoid) the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. They’re two of our top-rated smartwatches for their fitness, health and other smart features. Audio Intelligence is either an added bonus (it’s free) or something you can ignore altogether.

But if you do decide to venture into this brave fresh world of AI notetakers, my suggestion would be to use Siri Recap intentionally rather than leaving it running all day.

Turn it on before a work meeting, a doctor’s appointment or another conversation where you might want a few notes to jog your memory later. Just make sure everyone involved knows it’s enabled and is comfortable with it, and that you’re not relying on it for crucial information.

If the stakes are high, have a backup — whether that’s your own notes or a recording — lest you risk coming home with the wrong kid.

The Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero. The $399 Flipper One is a pocket Linux computer focused on networking, with delivery estimated for July 2027. But it isn’t simply an updated version of the Flipper Zero. It’s a very different animal and a much more serious bit of kit.

The thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use. You could fire it up and turn the volume down on the TV at your parents’ place, see the radio waves coming from your car’s key fob, and copy hotel room key cards.

Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited.

In a recent development, it could do a lot, there wasn’t a steep learning curve, and you didn’t need to buy anything else. Did the fake videos on TikTok from people claiming they could change the prices at gas stations (I wish!) or start cars remotely help make the Zero more popular?

It has been revealed that unfortunately, yes. But what made it successful was that it packed a lot of power into a package that was small, fun, affordable, and easy to use.

If the Flipper Zero, with its NFC, RFID, sub-GHz, and IR, was kindergarten, the Flipper One is a college degree: a pocket Linux computer focused on networking.

This is reflected in the price. You can pick up a Zero for $169, while the Flipper One is $399.

What this buys you is the Flipper One base computer with a 256 × 144 grayscale LCD, Rockchip RK3576 8-core ARM SoC with NPU, a low-power MCU for handling the LCD and user interface, 8GB of LPDDR5 RAM, 64GB of UFS 2.2 storage, and a microSD slot.

If that $399 feels like a lot, it’s worth keeping in mind that, according to Flipper, the price only covers production costs and that the RAM and UFS storage account for at least half of the total hardware cost.

If you think this is a lot, you could spend a lot more. Adding a LoRa, SDR, or 5G module will push the total up a lot higher. And if you want all three modules, you’re looking at $759 for the Flipper One Ultimate Bundle.

Also: The Flipper One is the Linux cyberdeck I wish my Raspberry Pi could be.

The reception has been strong enough that pledges have flown past the $300,000 goal that Flipper initially set, with over 24,000 backers pledging over $13 million. Close to 5,300 backers have gone for the Ultimate Bundle, compared to just over 4,300 choosing the bare Flipper One.

This suggests that backers really want the radio capabilities that this newly introduced platform offers.

If you want one, this crowdfunding run is a good time to get one because it’s a Kickstarter Special slashing 25% off an estimated retail price of $550.

The response over on Reddit has been a little more subdued, with some being taken aback by the price of the Zero’s bigger sibling.

Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years.

As someone who homebrews a lot of electronics, I’m going to say that the price is justified, and this project goes far beyond something you could put together with a Raspberry Pi and some code.

Industry observers note that the Flipper One campaign runs until Dec. 17, 2026, with delivery estimated for July 2027.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that this is a Kickstarter pledge, not a purchase, and that rewards aren’t guaranteed. Flipper also says on the Kickstarter page that component shortages are the biggest risk to the project and that they “could cause significant delays to production and delivery.” It also says that if RAM prices continue to rise, it cannot “rule out adjusting some product specifications, including reducing the amount of RAM.”.

Also: Is the Flipper Zero the best multi-tool for hacking?

And the good news here is that I’ve seen several analysts predicting that RAM prices will begin to go down in 2027 as demand eases off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that over the last month, I fell in love with a latest game that’s actually old. It’s happened to me before, but Nintendo’s Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake drove that feeling home in a surprising way. How did Nintendo get me to fall so deeply in love again with a game I’ve already played? And why is it still winning me over, even with Grand Theft Auto 6 here?

It has been revealed that I’m still thinking about (and playing) Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2, even with GTA 6 loaded up at home. GTA’s universe overwhelms me, but it also makes me appreciate Ocarina’s focus and clarity. And it’s also another incredible graphics showcase for what the Switch 2 is capable of. Yes, GTA 6 is jaw-dropping. But so are Ocarina’s 60fps vistas and details. Zelda pioneered 3D gaming before GTA ever went 3D.

Sources indicate that I also can’t stop thinking about what a game like this means for Nintendo’s next wave of Switch 2 games, and a future Zelda game. Zelda’s previous games became increasingly open world, full of multiplying tasks and larger maps. It can get overwhelming. Ocarina of Time’s focus is smaller, but still tangled and immersive. Can the two concepts feed off each other? Will Ocarina help rethink where the next Zeldas are heading? And, maybe, where other open-world games are heading, too?

At Ocarina’s launch, I met in person with Nintendo’s producers for the remake, Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi, to discuss what it all meant and how the remake bridged the gap between the “old Zelda” and “newly introduced Zelda.” Aonuma has been a producer for Zelda games since the original Ocarina of Time, and Fujibayashi directed both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

For this project, they brought on staffers who’d worked on Tears of the Kingdom, many of them much younger developers.

According to recent reports, “In fact, some of them hadn’t even played the original Ocarina of Time on Nintendo 64,” says Aonuma. “We also saw this as a really interesting opportunity for this younger staff to make discoveries on the course of this project that they could bring forward on future Zelda projects that they might work on as well.”.

There are a lot more subtle visual clues, I found, even than what I remembered in Nintendo’s last two Zelda games.

Industry observers note that “When we were working on Tears of the Kingdom, we had this very high capacity to express all kinds of details and this feeling of immersion in the world, and that’s something I think was a massive influence on the remake,” states Aonuma. “Whether it’s a visual detail that you might spot from a distance that you may not have in the original, that could be something that draws the player in and suddenly gives them the motivation to explore.”.

According to recent reports, what worked wonders, I found, was the quiet, subtle immersion, especially when exploring dungeons or figuring out solutions I’d forgotten decades ago. I had to study the environment for clues.

That’s the magic ingredient: a throughline in the Zelda games that Fujibayashi says is “the idea of exploration and discovery.”.

Fujibayashi appreciates how the visual tools have improved, even since Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom on the original Switch.

“A system that lets you share a high, dense volume of information visually provides new ways of giving clues to the player: They can use their sight to gather the information they need to do some of the puzzle solving,” he notes. “Even if you compare the graphics to Breath of the Wild, it looks slightly more realistic now. And that impacts how we approach puzzle solving and puzzle creation.”.

I think about Grand Theft Auto as the new benchmark for immersion and graphic detail, but I’m also finding that a lot of GTA’s discoveries are made through pop-up interaction graphics that let you know when something can be activated. Ocarina of Time doesn’t always do this. And I also can’t help but wonder: Could the Switch 2 achieve a way to run a new wave of impressive games using optimized graphics, even something on a level like Grand Theft Auto’s latest?

Or, rather, what if Nintendo aims for a new level of hyper-immersion in its games going forward, learning from Ocarina of Time?

Sources indicate that speaking of immersion, I kind of wish I could hold my Joy-Con up and use it like an ocarina in the latest game. You can’t, although you can use the controllers to play notes or hum or play a tune into the built-in microphone using your own voice or instrument — something lots of people have been showing off online. But the Joy-Con-as-ocarina idea almost became a reality.

According to recent reports, “To be honest, we did briefly think about doing exactly that, but then we also considered how difficult it is to turn the Joy-Con into something that’s going to make a sound that is faithful, and then also how to develop that into the application inside of the game as well,” says Aonuma. “What we ultimately decided to do instead was to have this audio recognition feature in the software where you can use any instrument that you would like, whether it’s analog or digital, and you can play these themes and have the effect in the game and experience that way.”.

In a recent development, what I’m really hoping for is a Majora’s Mask remake, the second N64 Zelda game that built off Ocarina’s graphics engine. Nintendo could do the same here, although Nintendo wouldn’t answer my questions about Majora’s Mask during my interview.

I’m still unlocking all the little secrets in Ocarina of Time, sinking into the world as I go. And when I play the notes on my Switch, I imagine I’m playing that ocarina. After playing this Zelda game, I wonder what Nintendo could do with that same level of detail for Mario’s return on the Switch 2, almost 10 years after the last upcoming 3D Mario game on the Switch. We might know the answer to that soon enough.

Also: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI training.

In a recent development, fresh to Google’s AI Mode is an option known as temporary threads. By choosing this setting, any searches you conduct in AI mode are detached from your own Google account and history. Your temporary searches won’t be affected by your past preferences or chats. They won’t be impacted by any personalization you’ve set up through your account. And they won’t be saved to your chat history. The goal here is to prevent anyone else, including Google, from accessing your conversations in this mode.

In a recent development, this option is right now rolling out around the world in all languages to Google search on both desktop and mobile browsers. You can run a temporary thread on any device and in any browser.

Try this for yourself: Head to the regular Google search page and click the button on the search field for AI Mode. You should then see an icon with a pen hovering over a dotted circle. If you don’t see it, you may have to run a search to get started. On the results page, you should then spot the icon.

Hover over the icon, and the tooltip will say: “Start temporary thread.” Click the icon on the left to start a new thread. Now, any conversation you kick off will be temporary and unconnected to your account. But you don’t have to stick with just plain old text. Select the plus icon to upload an image or file. Select the microphone icon to speak instead of type.

Certain limitations are in effect with a temporary thread. Specifically, you can’t do any of the following:.

It has been revealed that are these temporary threads truly private? Here’s what Google says:.

Google will still collect data and use data that is not associated with your account, including to keep our services working smoothly and safely and to support business operations.”.

Google also warns that your browser may still save your history if you visit a website within a temporary thread. Data could still be collected by the sites you visit and the services those sites use, including Google services like Google Analytics.

Sources indicate that for those reasons, you should still be cautious about the information you share even in a temporary thread. But certainly, this option provides greater privacy and protection than a regular AI Mode search.

I’m glad to see Google finally offering this option through its AI Mode searches. This marks the second privacy-friendly development in recent days from the search giant. On Tuesday, Google confirmed that it would be rolling out upcoming settings through which you could opt out of AI model training without losing access to your chat history.

Breaking: Private markets are more accessible than ever for investors. Getting out is another matter

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Retail investors are lining up to back private funds.
  • PwC research has found that 77% of fund distributors surveyed said access to private markets is becoming crucial or very important to what they strategy to offer clients, but just 15% of asset managers said they provide comprehensive education for retail investors.
  • Unlike the public markets retail investors are more used to, some private-market vehicles limit when investors can get their money back to set repurchase windows, and even then may return only part of what they request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Retail investors are lining up to back private funds. But education on how restrictive these funds can be, particularly on when and how much money they can get back, may not be keeping pace with the influx of latest capital.

PwC research has found that 77% of fund distributors surveyed said access to private markets is becoming crucial or very important to what they strategy to offer clients, but just 15% of asset managers said they provide comprehensive education for retail investors.

Unlike the public markets retail investors are more used to, some private-market vehicles limit when investors can get their money back to set repurchase windows, and even then may return only part of what they request.

A spike in redemption requests at several private-credit funds earlier this year exposed the tension between giving investors regular opportunities to cash out and holding assets that can be difficult to sell promptly.

Blackstone restricted withdrawals from its $79 billion flagship nontraded BCRED private credit fund to 5% of shares in June, after redemption requests hit 10% during the second quarter. Apollo also capped withdrawals in its Apollo Debt Solutions vehicle at 5% after second-quarter redemption requests surged to almost 17%. Blue Owl, Morgan Stanley and Partners Group also limited investor withdrawals from some of their funds.

Limitations on redemptions are a key trade-off in structures such as LTAFs in the U.K., ELTIFs in the EU and interval funds in the U.S., which broaden access to less-liquid assets.

It's emerged as a major pressure point as those structures come under closer scrutiny.

"Private markets can have very different characteristics from the products many wealth clients are used to, particularly around liquidity, valuations and holding periods," stated Albertha Charles, global asset and wealth management leader at PwC.

"Investors and advisers need to understand how these products work, including their liquidity and valuation characteristics, so they can make informed decisions about whether they are appropriate.".

It has been revealed that pwC's 2026 Asset Management Revolution report, published Nov. 23, surveyed 250 asset managers, 100 institutional investors and 100 distributors across 36 countries and regions. More than half of respondents represented firms with over $20 billion in assets under management.

Among the study's key findings, education and liquidity are seen as the main hurdles as private markets reach a broader investor base. Distributors remarked better advisor and client education would help expand access, while liquidity, lock-ups and suitability requirements remain major barriers. Private equity and private credit were also the areas where distributors saw some of the biggest gaps in advisor knowledge.

Private credit appears likely to draw the strongest demand — two-thirds (66%) of distributors expect it to lead client interest in private markets, compared with 46% for private equity.

Regulators in several major markets are creating structures to widen access to long-term and illiquid assets. The U.K. uses long-term asset funds, or LTAFs, while the EU's European long-term investment funds, known as ELTIFs, can be marketed across member states.

In the U.S., interval funds provide periodic, rather than daily, liquidity. Singapore, Japan and Hong Kong have also taken steps to broaden retail or listed access to private assets. The frameworks differ, but all aim to make less-liquid investments workable within existing distribution, suitability and liquidity requirements.

Yen Sum, global chair of the private capital practice at Latham & Watkins, and a member of its executive committee, mentioned access to private-market funds is generally limited to investors who certify they are qualified or sophisticated.

She told CNBC on Thursday that the key issue for investor education centers on how private assets differ in liquidity, maturities and return-of-capital terms, and how higher rates can pressure leveraged companies — rather than simply whether regulation should curb access.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The flood is too much for Tidal. The music streaming app revealed on Tuesday that it is banning all tracks it determines to be entirely AI-generated. The platform noted it’s making the move after being increasingly inundated with non-human music. As of Dec. 9, Tidal will no longer accept or host fully AI-generated tracks.

The app also noted distributors, such as DistroKid, TuneCore, CD Baby and others, would not be allowed to deliver wholly AI-generated music.

Recent findings suggest that according to Tidal, 43% of tracks distributed to the app over the past three months were completely AI-generated, including 60% of the music submitted on Nov. 6 alone. Tidal remarked the affected tracks were labeled as AI and removed from the royalty pool, which is the pot of subscription and ad revenue paid out to rights holders.

According to recent reports, before Tuesday’s action, Tidal had tried to lessen AI’s influence by identifying, labeling and demonetizing AI tracks, as outlined in its AI policy. But amid the growing influx of AI music, representatives for the app mentioned it was time for “a more drastic change.”.

Tidal remarked there are 27 million tracks in its catalog that are 100% AI, but 96% of them have not been streamed at all in the past three months. Those 27 million tracks make up 6.3% of Tidal’s entire listings.

The manufacturer has removed more than 65,000 tracks flagged for artist-name impersonation.

Sources indicate that some AI help is permitted. Musical tracks where the maker used AI assistance but did not rely on it to generate the entire track will be allowed on the platform. Tidal uses ⁠Ircam Amplify to detect AI.

A Tidal representative told CNET that the app does not set a maximum amount of AI assistance that can be used to make tracks, and affirmed that only tracks that are deemed 100% AI-generated would be removed.

Read more: I Only Listened to AI Music for a Week. It Was Terrible, but Not for the Reason You Think.

“Tidal will always fight for artists to get paid more,” the firm remarked in its announcement. “Everything in this update comes back to that. If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for or copied by someone pretending to be you.”.

It has been revealed that generating music with AI is increasingly easy with online tools. The AI song-generation platform Suno can create songs using only text prompts. With Google’s Lyria, you can use photos or text prompts to generate tracks up to 3 minutes long.

Industry observers note that AI music also is not just about creating hit songs. Some industries need affordable music for short-form videos, games, apps and retail spaces, and they are increasingly turning to AI to supply it.

But streaming apps and other companies are fighting back against AI slop, which refers to often poor-quality AI-generated social media posts, articles, music, videos and images inundating the internet in an attempt to generate click-and-stream revenue.

In a recent development, youTube recently rolled out a new labeling system to indicate which music is AI-generated. Deezer provides a free tool listeners can use to see which tracks are AI-generated. Spotify is labeling which musicians are AI and which are human. Apple is flagging AI-generated music so listeners can spot it.

💡 Key Takeaways
